Ekadhammavagga Ekadhammasutta: The Discourse on a Single Dhamma At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there is this one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. [The bhikkhus asked: “And what, Bhante, is that one thing? “Bhikkhus, it is loving-kindness (*mettā*). Loving-kindness, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. [The bhikkhus asked: “And how, Bhante, is loving-kindness developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning? “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself—he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that loving-kindness is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught this one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. And what is that one thing? Loving-kindness. Loving-kindness, friends, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. And how, friends, is loving-kindness developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... [as above] ...without ill will. It is in this way, friends, that loving-kindness is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of non-returning. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having understood the meaning of this statement, recited these verses: “Loving-kindness is the one thing that the Buddha, the All-Knowing, the Knower of the World, has proclaimed as leading to the fruit of non-returning. By means of loving-kindness, a bhikkhu who is diligent abandons the five lower fetters and is no longer subject to rebirth in the womb.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying:
“Bhikkhus, there is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, yields great fruit and brings great benefit.”
What is that one thing?
Mindfulness of breathing.
And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?
"Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out.
Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I am breathing in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I am breathing out long’."
Breathing in short, he understands: “I am breathing in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I am breathing out short. He trains thus:
“Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in”; he trains thus: “Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus:
“Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in”; he trains thus: “Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out.”
‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing rapture, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘experiencing the mental formations, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing the mental formations, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Calming the mental formations, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘calming the mental formations, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘gladdening the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘gladdening the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in concentrating the mind"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in liberating the mind"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out liberating the mind.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence."
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence’;
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating fading away’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating fading away’;
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating cessation.’
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
It is when mindfulness of breathing has been developed and cultivated in this way, monks, that it is of great fruit and great benefit. Thus was the first [discourse].
Saṃyutta Nikāya 54.2 (SN 54.2, PTS SN v 312) 1. Ekadhamma-vagga Bojjhaṅga-sutta “Monks, there is one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship.
What is that one thing? The seven factors of enlightenment. These seven factors of enlightenment, monks, when developed and cultivated, lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship.”
“Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.
And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?

Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment accompanied by mindfulness of breathing, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment.”

“He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena accompanied by mindfulness of breathing … [and so on] … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by mindfulness of breathing, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment. Monks,
mindfulness of breathing thus developed and cultivated is of great fruit and great benefit.”

Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out...
[as before] ...he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’"

The third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 54.4 (SN 54.4, PTS SN v 313)
1. The Chapter on a Single Dhamma:
The First Discourse on the Fruits “Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.”
"And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully... [as above] ..."
‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ he trains himself; ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment,’ he trains himself.
Thus developed, monks, thus cultivated, mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.

When mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and thus cultivated, one of two fruits may be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of non-returning.
"Full knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 54.5 (SN 54.5, PTS SN v 314).
1. The Chapter on a Single Dhamma;
Second Discourse on the Fruits:
“Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.”
"And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully... [as above] ... "
‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
Thus developed, monks, thus cultivated, mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.
When mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and thus cultivated, seven fruits and seven benefits may be expected.
What are the seven fruits and seven benefits?
One attains final knowledge early in this very life;
or, if one does not attain final knowledge early in this very life... [the remaining fruits follow].
Then, at the time of death, one attains final knowledge; or,
if one does not attain final knowledge in this very life, nor at the time of death, then,
with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes one who attains Nibbāna in the interval.
He is one who attains nibbāna upon landing;
he is one who attains nibbāna without exertion;
he is one who attains nibbāna with exertion.
“He becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Monks, when mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and cultivated in this way, these seven fruits and seven benefits are to be expected.
The fifth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 54.6 (SN 54.6, PTS SN v 314) 1. Ekadhammavagga Ariṭṭha Sutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when one thing is developed and cultivated, it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. What one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. When mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated, bhikkhus, it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One spoke this brief statement: ‘Bhikkhus, when one thing is developed and cultivated, it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. What one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. When mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated, bhikkhus, it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. Now, friends, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship? [The venerable Ānanda then explained the development of mindfulness directed to the body in detail. “Friends, it is in such a way that mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. Then the venerable Ariṭṭha approached the venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of developing and cultivating mindfulness directed to the body? “Friend, the purpose of developing and cultivating mindfulness directed to the body is tranquility of mind; the purpose of tranquility of mind is non-regret; the purpose of non-regret is joy; the purpose of joy is rapture; the purpose of rapture is happiness; the purpose of happiness is concentration; the purpose of concentration is knowing and seeing things as they really are; the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they really are is disenchantment; the purpose of disenchantment is dispassion; the purpose of dispassion is liberation; the purpose of liberation is knowledge and vision of liberation. It is for this purpose, friend, that mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated. Then the venerable Ariṭṭha, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the venerable Ānanda, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the venerable Ariṭṭha had left, the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, including the conversation with the venerable Ariṭṭha. “Good, good, Ānanda! It is fitting for you to explain the meaning of my brief statement in such a way. For, Ānanda, it is in this way that mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the realization of the fruit of arahantship. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is the first discourse on the one thing in the First Chapter on the One Thing. Thus was the section on the one thing completed. [End of Saṁyutta Nikāya 54.6]
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One … [as before] … said this:
“Bhikkhus, do you develop mindfulness of breathing?”
When this was said, the Venerable Ariṭṭha said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I develop mindfulness of breathing.
"But how, Ariṭṭha, do you develop mindfulness of breathing?"

“Venerable sir, sensual desire for past sensual pleasures has been abandoned by me; sensual desire for future sensual pleasures has vanished from me; and regarding internal and external phenomena, my perception of repulsion has been thoroughly removed.
Thus, mindful I shall breathe in, and mindful I shall breathe out.
It is in this way, venerable sir, that I develop mindfulness of breathing.”
“‘Ariṭṭha, this mindfulness of breathing exists; I say it is not non-existent.
However, Ariṭṭha, listen to how mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail, and attend closely; I shall speak.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ariṭṭha replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And how, Ariṭṭha, is mindfulness of breathing fulfilled in detail?
Here, Ariṭṭha, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out.
Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’ … [and so on] …
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
In this way, Ariṭṭha, mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail.
The sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 54.7 (SN 54.7, PTS SN v 315) 1. Ekadhammavagga Mahākappina Sutta At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Mahākappina addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied to him. The Venerable Mahākappina said this: “Friends, when a bhikkhu possesses one quality, he may be expected to realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the fourfold analytical knowledge, and having realized it, to dwell in it. What single quality? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. When a bhikkhu possesses this one quality, he may be expected to realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the fourfold analytical knowledge, and having realized it, to dwell in it. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Mahākappina: “But, friend Kappina, how does a bhikkhu who possesses this one quality realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the fourfold analytical knowledge, and having realized it, dwell in it? “Here, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. Having emerged from the first jhāna, he directs his mind to the knowledge and vision of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is called the first analytical knowledge that he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, and having realized it, dwells in it. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas... Having emerged from the second jhāna, he directs his mind to the knowledge and vision of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn... and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is called the second analytical knowledge that he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, and having realized it, dwells in it. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas... Having emerged from the third jhāna, he directs his mind to the knowledge and vision of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn... and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is called the third analytical knowledge that he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, and having realized it, dwells in it. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas... Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. His heart is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. This is called the fourth analytical knowledge that he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, and having realized it, dwells in it. “Thus, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu who possesses this one quality realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the fourfold analytical knowledge, and having realized it, dwells in it. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Mahākappina: “But, friend Kappina, how does a bhikkhu who possesses this one quality gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life? “Here, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the abandoning of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purification of mindfulness through equanimity. “Thus, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu who possesses this one quality gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Mahākappina: “But, friend Kappina, how does a bhikkhu who possesses this one quality become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life? “Here, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, he, by completely transcending the earth element, dwells with a mind imbued with the water element, and he perceives the water element both internally and externally. Just as if there were a blue, yellow, red, white, or brown cloth, smooth and well-dyed, laid out on a wooden plank, and a man with good eyesight were to examine it, so too, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... dwells with a mind imbued with the water element, and he perceives the water element both internally and externally. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise... he, by completely transcending the water element, dwells with a mind imbued with the fire element, and he perceives the fire element both internally and externally. Just as if there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals without flame or smoke, and a man with good eyesight were to examine it, so too, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... dwells with a mind imbued with the fire element, and he perceives the fire element both internally and externally. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise... he, by completely transcending the fire element, dwells with a mind imbued with the air element, and he perceives the air element both internally and externally. Just as if there were a strong east wind, and a man with good eyesight were to examine it, so too, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... dwells with a mind imbued with the air element, and he perceives the air element both internally and externally. “Again, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise... he, by completely transcending the air element, dwells with a mind imbued with the space element, and he perceives the space element both internally and externally. Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākappina was sitting not far from the Blessed One, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Mahākappina sitting not far away, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do you see any wavering or quivering of this bhikkhu’s body?
“Venerable sir, whether we see that venerable one sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha or sitting alone in private, we do not see any wavering or quivering of that venerable one’s body.”
“Bhikkhus, when that concentration has been developed and cultivated, there is no trembling or quivering of the body,
nor is there any trembling or quivering of the mind.
That bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is one who gains that concentration at will, without difficulty, and without trouble.”
"And of what concentration, monks, is it that through its being developed and cultivated there is neither trembling nor shaking of the body, nor trembling nor shaking of the mind?

It is, monks, of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing that, through its being developed and cultivated, there is neither trembling nor shaking of the body, nor trembling nor shaking of the mind."

And how, bhikkhus, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, does there come to be neither trembling nor quivering of the body, nor trembling nor quivering of the mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him, he breathes in mindful and breathes out mindful... Saṃyutta Nikāya 54.8 (SN 54.8, PTS SN v 316) 1. Ekadhamma-vagga The Simile of the Lamp “Bhikkhus, there is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of the supreme security from bondage. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. This, bhikkhus, is that one thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of the supreme security from bondage. [The Buddha then spoke further: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take a lamp and enter a house that was dark for many years. As soon as he entered, the lamp would dispel the darkness and bring light. In the same way, bhikkhus, when mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated, it leads to the attainment of the supreme security from bondage. And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of the supreme security from bondage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally... He dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body—‘Arising, arising’; ‘passing away, passing away’; ‘arising and passing away, arising and passing away. Just as a person with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, might see fish swimming about or turtles crawling along, so too, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... externally... both internally and externally... contemplating its nature of arising... its nature of passing away... its nature of arising and passing away. This, bhikkhus, is how mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of the supreme security from bondage.”
“Monks, concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.
And how, monks, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?
Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.”
Thus, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long";
... pe ... he trains himself: "I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment," he trains himself: "I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment."
"Monks, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and cultivated in this way, it is of great fruit and great benefit.
Monks, even before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I dwelt frequently in this very dwelling.
While I dwelt frequently in this dwelling, monks, neither my body nor my eyes grew weary."
And through non-clinging, my mind was liberated from the taints.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May neither my body nor my eyes grow weary, and may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging," [he should attend to the perception of light.]
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May those memories and intentions of mine connected with the household life be abandoned," [then he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive," [he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive," [he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive," [he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive," [he should attend to this].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"May I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the unrepulsive and the repulsive," [he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be attended to thoroughly.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

"May I, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion," [then he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

"With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, may I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness," [then he should attend to this concentration].
This very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be thoroughly attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
"With the fading away of rapture, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and may I experience happiness with the body," [he should attend to this].
‘May I, having attained the third jhāna, dwell therein— that which the noble ones describe as “dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous”—
then this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

‘By the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and by the previous disappearance of joy and grief, may I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity’—
this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

‘By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] “space is infinite,” may I enter and dwell in the base of infinite space’—
this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
‘Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, [perceiving] “consciousness is infinite,” may I enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness’—
this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:
‘Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] “there is nothing,” may I enter and dwell in the base of nothingness’—
this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

‘Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, may I enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,’ this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish:

‘Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, may I enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling’—this very concentration through mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to.

When this concentration through mindfulness of breathing has been thus developed and cultivated, if one feels a pleasant feeling, one understands: ‘It is impermanent’; one understands: ‘It is not clung to’; one understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’
If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent," he understands: "It is not clung to," he understands: "It is not delighted in.
If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent," he understands: "It is not clung to," he understands: "It is not delighted in.
If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;
if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
Feeling a feeling that ends with the body, he understands: "I feel a feeling that ends with the body"; feeling a feeling that ends with life, he understands: "I feel a feeling that ends with life."
‘With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, not being delighted in, will become cool right here,’ he understands.
Just as, monks, an oil lamp might burn in dependence on oil and a wick, and with the exhaustion of that very oil and wick it would go out for lack of fuel; so too...
In the same way, monks, when a monk experiences a feeling that has its limit in the body, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has its limit in the body’;
when he experiences a feeling that has its limit in life, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has its limit in life.’
‘With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, not being delighted in, will become cool right here,’ he understands.
Thus it was said.
The eighth. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 54.9 (SN 54.9, PTS SN v 320).
1. The Chapter on a Single Dhamma:
The Discourse at Vesālī.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

Now on that occasion the Blessed One was giving a discourse on foulness in many ways to the bhikkhus, speaking in praise of foulness and speaking in praise of the development of the meditation on foulness.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for half a month.
No one should approach me, except for a single person who brings almsfood.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, and no one approached the Blessed One except for the single person who brought almsfood.

Then those bhikkhus, thinking, "The Blessed One speaks in many ways on the subject of foulness; he praises foulness; he praises the cultivation of foulness," dwelt devoted to the practice of the cultivation of foulness in its many forms and aspects.
Being repelled, humiliated, and disgusted by this body, they sought for an assassin.
Ten bhikkhus took their own lives on the same day; twenty... [and so on] ...thirty bhikkhus took their own lives on the same day.
Then, at the end of that half-month, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why is it that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus appears as if diminished?"
“However, venerable sir, because the Blessed One has in many ways spoken a discourse on foulness to the bhikkhus,
praised foulness, and praised the development of foulness, they dwell devoted to the practice of the development of foulness in its many aspects and modes.
Being repelled, humiliated, and disgusted by this body, they seek for an assassin.”
“Ten bhikkhus take up the knife on the same day; twenty bhikkhus… thirty bhikkhus take up the knife on the same day.
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain another method so that this Saṅgha of bhikkhus might be established in final knowledge.
“Therefore, Ānanda, assemble all the bhikkhus who dwell in dependence on Vesālī in the assembly hall.”
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Having gathered all the bhikkhus who were living in dependence on Vesālī in the assembly hall,
he approached the Blessed One and, having arrived, said this to him:
“Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has assembled.
Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems timely.
Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"This concentration through mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated state of happiness;
it causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to be stilled."
“Just as, monks, when in the last month of summer the dust and dirt have been stirred up, a great unseasonal cloud instantly makes it disappear and settles it; even so, monks,
when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, it is a peaceful and sublime state, refreshing and pleasant,
which instantly makes whatever evil, unwholesome states have arisen disappear and settles them.”

And how, monks, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes peaceful and sublime, a refreshing and blissful abiding, and causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and be stilled?
Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, being mindful, one breathes in; being mindful, one breathes out... [and so on] ... one trains thus:
“I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment”; one trains thus: “I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
Monks, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way, it is peaceful and sublime.
“And it is a dwelling that is unsurpassed and blissful; it causes whatever evil, unwholesome states have arisen to vanish on the spot and to be stilled.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 54.10 (SN 54.10, PTS SN v 322).
1. The Chapter on a Single Dhamma:
The Kīḷima Sutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā in the Bamboo Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kimila:
“Kimila, how is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?”
When this was said, the Venerable Kimila remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and a third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kimila:
“Kimbila, how is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?
For a third time, the Venerable Kimbila remained silent.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One:
“Now is the time for this, Blessed One; now is the time for this, Sugata.
May the Blessed One speak on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And how, Ānanda, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?”
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out...
[as above] ...he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out.’
"Thus developed, Ānanda, and thus cultivated, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, while breathing in long, understands: ‘I am breathing in long’; or while breathing out long, understands:
‘I am breathing out long’; or while breathing in short, understands: ‘I am breathing in short’; or while breathing out short, understands: ‘I am breathing out short’;"
‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body,’ he trains himself; ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body,’ he trains himself;
‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation,’ he trains himself; ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation,’ he trains himself.
At that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
Ānanda, I say that this, namely, inhalation and exhalation, belongs to a certain part of the body.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture,’ he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing rapture’; he trains thus:
‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure,’ he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus:
‘I shall breathe in experiencing mental formations,’ he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing mental formations.’
‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formations,’ he trains himself—
in this way, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
“I say, Ānanda, that this is one kind of feeling: namely, careful attention to in-breathing and out-breathing.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
On whatever occasion, Ānanda, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind,’ he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.’”
Gladdening the mind...
concentrating the mind...
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind.’
At that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, I do not say that there is the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind as mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence’ … [and so on] … ‘contemplating fading away’ … [and so on] … [he dwells on that occasion contemplating the mind as mind].
Contemplating cessation...
training thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ training thus:

‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment’—at that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Thus, having seen with wisdom that which is the abandoning of covetousness and dejection, he dwells having thoroughly looked on with equanimity.
Therefore, Ānanda, at that time a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were a great heap of dust at a crossroads.
If a cart or a chariot were to come from the eastern direction, it would simply crush that heap of dust;
if it were to come from the western direction...
or from the northern direction... [it would likewise crush it].

Just as a cart or a chariot coming from the southern direction would surely crush that heap of dust, even so, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in contemplation of the body as body surely crushes evil, unwholesome states; [and likewise] in regard to feelings... [and so on].
“Even while dwelling contemplating mind in mind … [and] phenomena in phenomena, one surely destroys evil, unwholesome states.
The tenth.
The First Chapter on the Single Dhamma.
Its summary verse:
The single dhamma, the enlightenment factor, and so forth.
And two pure fruits:
Ariṭṭha, Kappina, Dīpa,
Vesālī, and Kimila.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 54.11 (SN 54.11, PTS SN v 325) 2. Second Chapter: The Discourse at Icchānaṅgala "Monks, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, being tied to these five cords of sensual pleasure, are infatuated with them, attached to them, and find delight in them—these I do not consider to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and they do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood. But whatever ascetics or brahmins, being detached from these five cords of sensual pleasure, are not infatuated with them, not attached to them, and do not find delight in them—these I consider to be ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins, and they, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood."
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I wish to retreat for three months.”
“I am not to be approached by anyone, except for one who brings almsfood.
“Very well, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Blessed One, and indeed no one approached the Blessed One, except for one who brought almsfood.
Then, at the end of those three months, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the monks:
“Monks, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you:
‘Friend, by means of what dwelling did the ascetic Gotama mostly dwell during the rains residence?’—being thus questioned, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
‘Friends, the Blessed One mostly dwelt during the rains residence in the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatisamādhi).’”
In this case, monks, mindful I breathe in, mindful I breathe out.
Breathing in long, I know: ‘I am breathing in long’; breathing out long, I know: ‘I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, I know: ‘I am breathing in short’; breathing out short, I know: ‘I am breathing out short.’
“I understand: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’ … [and so on] … I understand:
‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ and I understand: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
For, monks, if one were speaking rightly, it is of this that one would speak.”
“It is called the noble abiding,” “it is called the divine abiding,” and “it is called the Tathāgata’s abiding.
Speaking rightly of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, one may say:
“It is called the noble abiding,” “it is called the divine abiding,” and “it is called the Tathāgata’s abiding.”

“Bhikkhus, for those bhikkhus who are trainees (*sekha*), who have not yet attained their goal, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

And for those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are arahants— whose taints are exhausted, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence,
and are completely liberated through final knowledge— the concentration of mindfulness of breathing [is likewise developed].”
When developed and cultivated, it leads both to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
For, monks, were one speaking rightly, one would say of this:
"It is a noble abiding," or "It is a divine abiding," or "It is an abiding of the Tathāgata."
“Speaking rightly, one might say of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing:
‘It is a noble abiding,’ ‘It is a divine abiding,’ and ‘It is an abiding of the Tathāgata. Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 54.12 (SN 54.12, PTS SN v 327) 2. Second Chapter Kaṅkheyyasutta (The Discourse on One Who Should Have Doubts) “Bhikkhus, one who has doubts about the Teacher, one who has doubts about the Dhamma, one who has doubts about the Saṅgha, one who has doubts about the training, one who has doubts about his companions in the holy life—one such as this is called a person who is ‘stuck in the middle,’ a person who is ‘mired in the mud,’ a person who has fallen into a state of ruin, a person who has come to a bad destination, a person who has entered upon a wrong path. “But, bhikkhus, one who has no doubts about the Teacher, one who has no doubts about the Dhamma, one who has no doubts about the Saṅgha, one who has no doubts about the training, one who has no doubts about his companions in the holy life—one such as this is called a person who is ‘unshakable,’ a person who is ‘steadfast,’ a person who has reached the goal, a person who has attained security from bondage, a person who has arrived at the right path.”
On one occasion the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Mahānāma the Sakyan...
He said this to the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya:
“Venerable sir, is that very dwelling of a trainee the same as the dwelling of a Tathāgata, or is the dwelling of a trainee one thing and the dwelling of a Tathāgata another?
“Friend Mahānāma, the dwelling of a trainee is not the same as the dwelling of a Tathāgata.”
"Friend Mahānāma, the dwelling of one in training is indeed one thing, and the dwelling of a Tathāgata is another.

Those monks who are still in training, friend Mahānāma, who have not yet attained their goal but dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, they dwell having abandoned the five hindrances.
Which five?"
They dwell having abandoned the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will,
the hindrance of sloth and torpor,
and the hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
They dwell having abandoned the hindrance of doubt.

Furthermore, friend Mahānāma, those bhikkhus who are trainees (*sekha*), who have not yet attained their goal, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—they too dwell having abandoned these five hindrances.
And as for those bhikkhus, friend Mahānāma, who are arahants, whose taints are exhausted, who have lived the holy life, and who have done what was to be done—
They have laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through perfect knowledge.
For them, the five hindrances have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
What are the five?
The hindrance of sensual desire has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like the stump of a palm tree, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future;
the hindrance of ill will has been abandoned … [and so on] … the hindrance of sloth and torpor …
The hindrance of restlessness and remorse...
the hindrance of doubt has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Those monks, friend Mahānāma, who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, and laid down the burden...
For those who have attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, and who are liberated through perfect knowledge— these five hindrances have been abandoned by them,
cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
It is by this method, friend Mahānāma, that it should be understood how this is so.
The dwelling of one in training is one thing; the dwelling of a Tathāgata is another.
Once, friend Mahānāma, on a certain occasion, the Blessed One was staying at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
There, friend Mahānāma, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for three months.
I am not to be approached by anyone, except for one who brings me almsfood.
“Very well, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, and indeed no one approached the Blessed One, except for one who brought him almsfood.
Then, friends, at the end of those three months, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you:
'Friends, with what kind of dwelling did the ascetic Gotama mostly dwell during the rains residence?'—being thus asked, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:"
“Friends, the Blessed One spent most of his rainy-season retreats in the concentration of mindfulness of breathing.
In this regard, monks, mindful I breathe in, mindful I breathe out.
Breathing in long, I know: ‘I am breathing in long’; breathing out long, I know: ‘I am breathing out long’... [and so on].
"I understand: 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; I understand: 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
For that, monks, which one speaking rightly would call a noble abiding, a divine abiding, and an abiding of the Tathāgata."
Speaking rightly of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, one may say:
"It is an Ariyan dwelling," or "It is a Brahma-dwelling," or "It is a Tathāgata-dwelling.

For those monks, bhikkhus, who are trainees (sekha), who have not yet attained their goal, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—it is for them that the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints (āsava).
But as for those monks, bhikkhus, who are arahants— whose taints are exhausted, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge— for them,
concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
For if anyone, monks, speaking rightly, were to say:
"This is an abiding of the noble ones," or "This is an abiding of Brahmā," or "This is an abiding of the Tathāgata"—
it is of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing that one would speak rightly.
"It is called the noble abiding, it is called the divine abiding, and it is called the Tathāgata’s abiding.
It is by this method, friend Mahānāma, that it should be understood how the abiding of one in training is one thing, and the abiding of a Tathāgata is another."

The First Discourse on Ānanda.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Is there, venerable sir, one thing which, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things;
and four things which, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and seven things which, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”
“There is, Ānanda, one thing which, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things;
four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things.”
“But what, venerable sir, is that one thing which, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things;
which four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and which seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”
“Ānanda, this one dhamma—concentration through mindfulness of breathing—when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.”
How, Ānanda, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness?

Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he understands: “I am breathing in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I am breathing out long” ... pe ... he trains thus:
“Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in”; he trains thus: “Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out.
Ānanda, at whatever time a bhikkhu, breathing in long, understands: “I am breathing in long,” or breathing out long, understands: “I am breathing out long”;
Or short... [and so on]...
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
At that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
Ānanda, I say that this is one aspect of the body, namely, inhalation and exhalation.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture,’ ‘experiencing pleasure’ … [and so on] … ‘experiencing the mental formations’ …;
‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formations,’ he trains; ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formations,’ he trains.
At that time, Ānanda, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
“Ānanda, I say that this is a certain kind of feeling: namely, the thorough attention directed toward in-breaths and out-breaths.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
On whatever occasion, Ānanda, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind,’ he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.’”

he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind.’
At that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, I do not say that there is the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension.
Therefore, Ānanda, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

On whatever occasion, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating impermanence... [or] contemplating fading away... [etc.]... [he dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world].
Contemplating cessation...
training thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ training thus:

‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment’—at that time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Thus, having seen with wisdom that which is the abandoning of covetousness and dejection, he dwells having thoroughly looked on with equanimity.
Therefore, Ānanda, at that time a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this manner, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
And how, Ānanda, are the four foundations of mindfulness developed and cultivated so that they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—
at that time, mindfulness is established and unconfused in that bhikkhu.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is established and unconfused, at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has been undertaken by the bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness;
at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches its full development in the bhikkhu.
Thus dwelling mindfully, he investigates, examines, and scrutinizes that phenomenon with wisdom.

Ānanda, at whatever time a bhikkhu, dwelling thus mindfully, investigates, examines, and scrutinizes that phenomenon with wisdom—at that time, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena has been aroused in that bhikkhu; [he develops] the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.

At that time, the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena; at that time, the bhikkhu’s development of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena reaches fulfillment.
As he investigates, scrutinizes, and examines that phenomenon with wisdom, unflagging energy is aroused in him.
Ānanda, at whatever time unflagging energy is aroused in a bhikkhu as he investigates, scrutinizes, and examines that phenomenon with wisdom—

At that time, the factor of enlightenment of energy is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time, the bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment of energy; at that time, the factor of enlightenment of energy reaches fulfillment through development in the bhikkhu.
When energy is aroused, non-sensual rapture arises.
At whatever time, Ānanda, non-sensual rapture arises in a bhikkhu whose energy is aroused—

At that time, the factor of enlightenment that is rapture is undertaken by the bhikkhu; at that time, the bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment that is rapture; at that time, the factor of enlightenment that is rapture reaches fulfillment through development in the bhikkhu.
When the mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil and the mind also becomes tranquil.
Ānanda, at whatever time the body of a bhikkhu whose mind is filled with rapture becomes tranquil and the mind also becomes tranquil—
At that time, the enlightenment factor of tranquility has been undertaken by the bhikkhu;
at that time, the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility; at that time, the enlightenment factor of tranquility reaches fulfillment through development in the bhikkhu.
When the body is tranquil and he is happy, his mind becomes concentrated.
Ānanda, at whatever time a bhikkhu’s mind becomes concentrated when his body is tranquil and he is happy—at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration has been undertaken by the bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of concentration; at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration reaches its full development in the bhikkhu.
He then maintains careful equanimity toward that well-concentrated mind.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu thoroughly looks on with equanimity at the mind thus concentrated—at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity is initiated in the bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity; at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches its full development in the bhikkhu.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu [thoroughly looks on with equanimity] regarding feelings... [and so forth].
He dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects— in this case,
a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is established and unconfused at that time.
At whatever time, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is established and unconfused—at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has been undertaken by the bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches fulfillment of its development in the bhikkhu.
(As with the first foundation of mindfulness, so it should be elaborated.)
Thus he thoroughly looks on with equanimity at the mind so well-composed.
Ānanda, at whatever time a bhikkhu thoroughly looks on with equanimity at the mind so well-composed, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused by that bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity; at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches fulfillment in development for that bhikkhu.
"Ānanda, when the four foundations of mindfulness are thus developed and thus cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
And how, Ānanda, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and how are they cultivated so that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment."
“He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … [and so on] … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
It is when the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and cultivated in this way, Ānanda, that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation.”

The Second Discourse to Ānanda Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Is there, Ānanda, a single dhamma that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four dhammas? Four..."
“Dhammas, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven dhammas; the seven dhammas, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two dhammas.
“Our dhammas, venerable sir, are rooted in the Blessed One... [and so on].
“There is, Ānanda, one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things;
four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things.
And what, Ānanda, is the one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things? [The Buddha continued: “Four things...”
Which one dharma, when developed and cultivated, fulfills seven dharmas; and which seven dharmas, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two dharmas?
Ānanda, the one dharma that is concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi), when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).

"When developed and cultivated, it fulfills true knowledge and liberation. This, Ānanda, is how concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that, when practiced frequently, it fulfills the foundation of mindfulness that is the contemplation of feelings in feelings. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... [as before] ...he dwells. In him, Ānanda, while he dwells thus, mindfulness regarding the mind is established to a great extent; his mind is undisturbed by sensual lust; he has overcome the mental state of ill will and hatred. This, Ānanda, is how concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that, when practiced frequently, it fulfills the foundation of mindfulness that is the contemplation of the mind in the mind. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... [as before] ...he dwells. In him, Ānanda, while he dwells thus, mindfulness regarding phenomena is established to a great extent; his mind is undisturbed by sensual lust; he has overcome the mental state of ill will and hatred. This, Ānanda, is how concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that, when practiced frequently, it fulfills the foundation of mindfulness that is the contemplation of phenomena in phenomena. It is in this way, Ānanda, that concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that, when practiced frequently, it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness."
"It is when, Ānanda, the seven factors of awakening have been developed and cultivated in this way that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
